title: Profit, Loss and Discount

references.label: GSSSB Laboratory Assistant Detailed Syllabus, Part A (Advt. 327/2025-26)

scientificNotes: General competitive-exam quantitative-aptitude topic; included to match the exam's Part A scope.
expression: Profit % = ((SP − CP) / CP) × 100    Loss % = ((CP − SP) / CP) × 100    SP = MP × (1 − Discount%/100)
explanation: Profit or loss is always calculated as a PERCENTAGE OF THE COST PRICE (CP), never of the selling price (SP) — this is the single most common source of error in profit-loss problems. Selling Price (SP) exceeding Cost Price (CP) gives a profit; SP below CP gives a loss. A separate, related chain: Marked Price (MP, the labelled/listed price) is reduced by a discount percentage to arrive at the actual Selling Price — so discount is calculated on MP, while profit/loss is calculated on CP; these are two DIFFERENT base quantities and must not be conflated.

variables.meaning: Cost price — what the seller paid to acquire/produce the item
Selling price — what the item is actually sold for
Marked price — the labelled/listed price before any discount
Percentage reduction from MP to reach SP

workedExample.scenario: An item marked at ₹500 is sold at a 20% discount. Its cost price was ₹350. Find the profit percentage.

commonMistakes: Calculating profit/loss percentage on the SELLING price instead of the COST price — the standard convention (and what these formulas assume) is always CP as the base.

Confusing 'marked price' with 'cost price' when computing discount versus profit — discount is off MP, profit/loss is relative to CP; treating them as the same base quantity gives a wrong final selling price or profit figure.
genZNote: Profit % always clocks in relative to CP — MP is just the sticker price flexing before the discount does its thing.
